title: Long-term care
teaches: How likely long-term care is and what it costs, what Medicare and Medicaid pay, and the choice between insurance and paying for it from savings

parts.title: The cost the plan leaves out

blocks.text: Every plan in the main course spent the same real amount each year until 95, the age it planned to. The real pattern is lumpier: spending usually drifts down through the seventies and eighties, and then, for many people, rises sharply at the end because of care. Help with bathing, dressing and eating, at home or in a facility, is long-term care, and Medicare mostly doesn't pay for it.[^adl]

Federal estimates suggest that about 70 percent of people turning 65 will need some long-term care, often a few months of help at home or after a hospital stay. About one in five will need it for more than five years. The average need is a couple of years, which savings can usually absorb; the risk is the small share of people who need care for many years, which can cost more than most savings.

blocks.caption: National median costs of a year of care in 2024, from the CareScout survey, rounded. Costs in the Seattle area run 20 to 40 percent higher.

options.title: A year of care, US medians

items.label: Home health aide, 44 hours a week

blocks.text: The home aide's figure is for 44 hours a week. Round-the-clock care at home, almost four times as many hours, costs far more than a nursing home. And a couple's plan that pays for one partner's care in a facility while the other stays in the house carries both costs at once: the care, and the household's ordinary spending.

**Medicare** pays for skilled nursing, care that needs a nurse or therapist, such as wound care or rehabilitation, after an inpatient hospital stay of three days or more, in full for 20 days and with a daily copay up to day 100, and for some skilled care at home. It doesn't pay for custodial care, help with daily living that someone without medical training could give, which makes up most long-term care, including most care for dementia.

**Medicaid** pays for most nursing home care in the US, but only once the person's savings are almost gone: in Washington, $2,000 for a single person. A spouse at home keeps the house and a car, and of the couple's other savings, a share up to about $160,000. Money given away in the five years before applying counts against eligibility, so that savings can't be handed to children just before applying: Medicaid delays cover by roughly a month for each month of care the gifts would have paid for. And Washington recovers what it paid from the estate after both spouses have died, the house included (the Washington branch's lesson on Apple Health).

**WA Cares**, Washington's payroll-funded care programme, pays up to $36,500 over a lifetime, adjusted for inflation, from July 2026, for those who paid into it long enough (the Washington branch's lesson on WA Cares).

**Savings** pay the rest. For a household with $1.5 million at 85, three years in a private nursing room at about $130,000 a year is a serious cost but not a ruinous one. For a household with $400,000, the same three years ends in Medicaid.

Traditional long-term care insurance pays a daily benefit for care, for a premium paid every year. The policies sold in the 1990s and 2000s were underpriced, and insurers have since raised premiums on existing holders many times, sometimes by 50 to 100 percent at once.[^ltc-mispricing] Few companies still sell them, and premiums for a 55-year-old couple run several thousand dollars a year.

Hybrid policies combine life insurance or an annuity with a care benefit. They cost a large single premium or ten years of premiums, can't be raised, and pay something either way: care if needed, a death benefit if not. Each dollar of premium buys less care cover than a traditional policy would.

A rough rule follows from these costs. Households with modest savings will spend down to Medicaid in a long illness whatever they do, so insurance mostly pays bills that Medicaid would otherwise have paid. Households with several million can pay for even five years, $650,000 or so, from savings. Insurance is worth most in the middle, from about $500,000 to $2 or $3 million, where a long stay could take most of what a surviving spouse needs.[^partnership]

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: About 70 percent of 65-year-olds will need some long-term care; about one in five for more than five years.
A nursing home costs about $110,000 to $130,000 a year at the US median, and more around Seattle.
Medicare pays only short skilled stays; Medicaid pays once savings are nearly spent.
Insurance matters most for households in the middle, protecting the spouse who stays at home.

blocks.caption: Four questions on long-term care
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: What does Medicare pay for a year in a nursing home needed because of dementia?
choices: Almost nothing: it is custodial care
items.why: Medicare covers skilled care for up to 100 days after a hospital stay, not long-term custodial care.

items.ask: When does Medicaid start paying for a single person's nursing home in Washington?
choices: Once their countable savings are down to about $2,000
items.why: Medicaid for long-term care has an asset limit; it pays only once savings are nearly spent.

items.ask: Why have many holders of traditional care insurance seen large premium increases?
choices: The policies were priced too low when sold
The policies converted to life insurance
items.why: Insurers expected many buyers to let their policies lapse, but almost all kept them, and the interest earned on reserves fell.

items.ask: Which household gains most from long-term care insurance?
choices: One with about $1 million, with a spouse to protect
items.why: Small estates reach Medicaid anyway, large ones can self-fund; the middle has most at risk.

summary: **Most people need some care, and one in five needs years of it.** About one in five 65-year-olds needs care for more than five years.
**Care is expensive.** A private nursing room costs about $128,000 a year at the US median.
**Medicare pays little of it.** Only short stays of skilled care after a hospital visit.
**Medicaid pays once savings are gone.** With protections for a spouse at home, and recovery from the estate.
**Insurance suits the middle.** Small estates reach Medicaid and large ones can pay; the middle has most to lose.

partnership.title: Partnership policies
partnership.text: Washington takes part in the long-term care partnership programme: for each dollar a qualifying policy pays out, a dollar of assets is protected if the holder later needs Medicaid. A $300,000 partnership policy that is used up lets its holder keep $302,000 instead of $2,000.

adl.title: Activities of daily living
adl.text: Insurers and Medicaid measure the need for care against six activities of daily living (ADLs): bathing, dressing, eating, using the lavatory, continence, and moving between bed and chair. Most policies start paying when the holder cannot do at least two of the six on their own, or has a severe cognitive impairment such as dementia.

ltc-mispricing.title: Why the 1990s policies failed
ltc-mispricing.text: Actuaries pricing early long-term care policies assumed about 5 percent of buyers would let their policies lapse each year, as happens with life insurance. In practice, fewer than 1 percent did: people who bought coverage for old age held on to it. Interest rates also fell for twenty years, cutting the return on the reserves insurers had set aside, and holders lived longer into the ages where dementia claims rise.
